name: Haitian state: First Empire → Republic of Haiti
description: The Haitian state from independence (1 January 1804) — the only successful slave revolution in history — through Dessalines's First Empire (1804-1806) to the Republic of Haiti, with the 1806-1820 north-south partition and the 1825 French indemnity documented.
ethical_notes: Haiti's founding is world-historical: the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue, the most profitable slave colony on earth, defeated France (and Spanish and British interventions) in a thirteen-year revolution (1791-1804) and abolished slavery unconditionally. The transition modelled here is NOT a clean succession: Dessalines's assassination at Pont-Rouge (17 October 1806) collapsed the First Empire into a north-south partition — Henry Christophe's State (from 1811, Kingdom) of Haiti in the north, Alexandre Pétion's Republic in the south — reunified under Jean-Pierre Boyer only in 1820; those parallel states are not yet modelled as entities. Two further truths, both kept: (1) in early 1804 Dessalines ordered the massacre of most of the remaining French population (est. 3,000-5,000 killed) — a documented atrocity born of a war of extermination waged against the formerly enslaved; (2) in 1825 France extorted, under threat of naval bombardment and reinvasion, an 'independence indemnity' of 150 million francs (later reduced to 90M) compensating former slaveholders — a ransom whose repayment (the 'double debt' with its financing interest) crippled Haiti's economy into the 20th century and is a live restitution question today. DATASET FLAG (ETHICS-017 §8): the predecessor entity #534 is named 'Repiblik Dayiti' but represents the 1804-1806 FIRST EMPIRE (expected name: Anpi an Ayiti / Empire d'Haïti); the successor #209 'Républik Ayiti' is a graphic hybrid (correct Kreyòl: Repiblik d Ayiti). Renames queued via the ETHICS-001 process; the chain uses the current names to resolve.

sources.citation: Dubois, L. 'Avengers of the New World: The Story of the Haitian Revolution' (Harvard University Press, 2004)
Dubois, L. 'Haiti: The Aftershocks of History' (Metropolitan Books, 2012)
James, C.L.R. 'The Black Jacobins: Toussaint L'Ouverture and the San Domingo Revolution' (1938; 2nd ed. Vintage, 1963)

links.description: The first independent Haitian state: independence declared at Gonaïves on 1 January 1804 by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who was proclaimed Emperor Jacques I in September-October 1804 (the First Empire). The 1805 constitution abolished slavery forever and declared all Haitians 'black' as a civic category — a radical anti-racist legal act.
links.ethical_notes: Entity name under review (it was an EMPIRE, not a republic — see chain-level dataset flag). The 1804 massacre of the remaining French colonists is part of this state's record, as is the revolution's unmatched emancipatory achievement.

links.description: Dessalines was assassinated by rivals at Pont-Rouge (17 October 1806); the empire collapsed into partition — Christophe's north (State, then Kingdom of Haiti, 1811-1820, with its own crown, nobility and the Citadelle) and Pétion's southern Republic — reunified under Boyer in 1820 as the Republic of Haiti, which then also ruled the whole island 1822-1844.
links.ethical_notes: The linear model compresses the 1806-1820 partition into notes because the parallel states are not yet entities (queued). The 1825 French indemnity extorted under naval threat burdened this republic for a century — see chain-level notes.

name: Montenegrin state: Зета → Црна Гора
description: The Montenegrin state tradition: from the medieval principality of Zeta (Balšić dynasty, 1360-1421) to Montenegro (Crna Gora) under the prince-bishops (vladike, from 1516), the Petrović-Njegoš dynasty (1697-1918), secular principality (1852) and kingdom (1910), until the contested annexation to Serbia/Yugoslavia in 1918.
ethical_notes: TERMINAL EVENT NOT MODELLED AS A LINK (see ETHICS-017 §5): the chain ends in 1918 because no suitable successor entity exists in the dataset — the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (1918-1929/41) is missing (queued; it is also needed by the Serbian trunk chain), and linking to socialist Yugoslavia (1945-) would be anachronistic. The end of Montenegrin statehood must not read as a peaceful fade-out: with King Nikola I in exile and the country under Serbian military occupation, the Podgorica Assembly (24-26 November 1918) — elected under conditions controlled by unionist forces — deposed the king and declared unconditional union with Serbia; opponents ('Greens', zelenaši) rose in the Christmas Uprising (7 January 1919, Cetinje), which was suppressed, with guerrilla resistance continuing into the mid-1920s. Historiography (Pavlović) describes the process as an annexation ('Balkan Anschluss'); Serbian unionist historiography described it as national unification — both framings are documented, per the no-single-version principle. Montenegro regained statehood only in 2006.

sources.citation: Roberts, E. 'Realm of the Black Mountain: A History of Montenegro' (Hurst / Cornell University Press, 2007)
Pavlović, S. 'Balkan Anschluss: The Annexation of Montenegro and the Creation of the Common South Slavic State' (Purdue University Press, 2008)

links.description: The principality of Zeta under the Balšić dynasty (1360-1421), successor of Duklja in the Adriatic hinterland; its dataset span ends with the passing of Balšić rule (1421); the Crnojević dynasty continued a shrinking Zeta from Žabljak and then Cetinje until Ottoman pressure ended secular rule (1496).
links.ethical_notes: The 1421-1515 interval (late Crnojević Zeta, Ottoman encroachment, the Cetinje printing press of 1493-96) falls between the two entities and is documented here rather than papered over.

links.description: Montenegro under the vladike (prince-bishops) of Cetinje, by tradition from 1516 (this entity's span starts 1515), hereditary in the Petrović-Njegoš line from 1697; internationally recognised as an independent principality at Berlin (1878); kingdom from 1910; occupied by Austria-Hungary 1916 and annexed to Serbia/the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918.
links.ethical_notes: UNMODELLED SUCCESSOR: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (entity queued). The 1918 Podgorica Assembly and the suppressed 1919 Christmas Uprising are the contested end of this state — see chain-level notes; this is an annexation documented in notes only because the successor entity does not yet exist, not because it was peaceful or uncontested.

name: Southern Italian kingdom: Regno di Napoli → Regno delle Due Sicilie → Regno d'Italia
description: The southern Italian state tradition: the Kingdom of Naples (1282-1816), merged with Sicily into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (December 1816) after the Congress of Vienna, conquered in 1860-61 during Italian unification and absorbed into the Kingdom of Italy.
ethical_notes: This chain complements the Italian unification trunk (Sardinia → Italy), giving the CONQUERED southern state its own succession line instead of leaving it as an unlinked footnote of the conqueror's chain. The 1860-61 transition was a conquest, not a voluntary merger: Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand (May 1860), the Piedmontese invasion through the Papal Marches, plebiscites held under occupation with open voting, the siege and fall of Gaeta (February 1861), and then the 'brigandage war' (1861-1865) — a counter-insurgency under martial law (Pica Law, 1863) with mass executions and villages destroyed, killing tens of thousands and inaugurating the 'Southern Question'. The 1816 merger itself abolished the Sicilian constitution of 1812 and Sicily's separate institutions, breeding the revolts of 1820 and 1848 — the Two Sicilies was itself a contested composite, not a harmonious unit.

sources.citation: Davis, J.A. 'Naples and Napoleon: Southern Italy and the European Revolutions, 1780-1860' (Oxford University Press, 2006)
Riall, L. 'The Italian Risorgimento: State, Society and National Unification' (Routledge, 1994)
Duggan, C. 'The Force of Destiny: A History of Italy Since 1796' (Allen Lane, 2007)

links.description: The Kingdom of Naples, the mainland southern kingdom from the Sicilian Vespers partition (1282) — Angevin, Aragonese, Spanish-viceregal, Austrian and Bourbon phases — ending with the Napoleonic decade (Joseph Bonaparte, Murat, 1806-1815) and the Bourbon restoration.
Ferdinand IV of Naples / III of Sicily merged his two crowns into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (8 December 1816) as Ferdinand I, under the post-Vienna restoration order.
links.ethical_notes: The merger unilaterally abolished the Sicilian constitution of 1812 and Palermo's institutional parity — a suppression of Sicilian autonomy that fuelled the 1820 and 1848 Sicilian revolutions; 'unification' here was dynastic consolidation, not consent.

links.description: Conquered in the Italian unification: Garibaldi's Thousand and the collapse of Bourbon Sicily and Naples (1860), plebiscites under occupation (October 1860), the fall of Gaeta (13 February 1861) ending Francis II's resistance, and absorption into the Kingdom of Italy proclaimed 17 March 1861.
links.ethical_notes: Followed by the brigandage war (1861-1865): martial law, the Pica Law, mass executions — tens of thousands killed in the conquered South. See also the Italian unification trunk chain's notes; both chains record the same events from the two sides.
